oil.e: From Middle English oyle, oile (“olive oil”), borrowed from Old French oile, from Latin oleum (“oil, olive oil”), from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”), from ἐλαία (elaía, “olive”). Supplanted Middle English ele (“oil”), from Old English ele (“oil”), also from Latin.
From Middle English oylen, from the noun (see above).

ointment.e: A later form (as if oint + -ment) of Middle English oinement, borrowed from Old French oignement (“an anointing”), from oigner, oindre, ongier (“to anoint”), from Latin ung(u)ō (“I anoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“to smear, anoint”). Partly displaced native Old English sealf, whence modern salve.
ointment.g: A viscous preparation of oils and/or fats, usually containing medication, used as a treatment or as an emollient.
